title: Manufacturing Account: Meaning, Purpose and Classification of Costs
summary: What a manufacturing account is, who prepares it, why it is prepared, and prime cost, factory overheads and factory cost.

p: A manufacturing account is an account prepared by a business that makes goods, to find the cost of producing the finished goods in the period. It is also called the production account, factory account or cost of production account. It is prepared by manufacturers, not traders. It comes before the trading account and is part of the final accounts.

A trading concern buys finished goods and sells them without changing them (a shop or supermarket). It has a trading account only. A manufacturing concern turns raw materials into finished goods (a bread factory, a textile mill). It needs a manufacturing account and a trading account.
Flow: raw materials → manufacturing account → cost of production → trading account → profit and loss account → balance sheet.

1. To find the cost of production (the factory cost). 2. To compare the cost of making goods with the cost of buying them (make-or-buy decisions). 3. For cost control: to watch production costs and find waste. 4. To give the figure used in the trading account (the cost of production takes the place of purchases). 5. To judge factory efficiency over time. 6. To help set selling prices and profit margins. 7. To give management a detailed breakdown of costs.

Prime cost (direct costs) is the cost directly connected with making the goods: raw materials used + direct labour (factory wages) + direct expenses (such as royalties for using a patent). Prime cost = raw materials used + direct labour + direct expenses.

Factory overheads (indirect costs) cannot be traced directly to a product: factory rent, power, lighting, insurance, depreciation of factory machinery, the factory supervisor's salary, factory repairs, lubricants and cleaning. Office, selling and administrative costs are NOT included.
Factory cost (cost of production) = prime cost + factory overheads, adjusted for work in progress.

title: Manufacturing Account: Format, Items and a Worked Example
summary: The layout of the manufacturing account, its items, a worked example, the link with the trading account, the three kinds of stock and common mistakes.

p: Study the table.

head: Manufacturing account for the year ended ...
rows: Add carriage inwards on raw materials
Less closing stock of raw materials
Factory overheads (rent, power, insurance, depreciation, supervisor, repairs)
Add opening work in progress; less closing work in progress
FACTORY COST OF PRODUCTION (to the trading account)

p: Opening stock of raw materials: raw materials in hand at the start. Purchases of raw materials. Carriage inwards on raw materials: the cost of bringing them in. Closing stock: raw materials still unused at the end. Raw materials consumed = opening stock + purchases (+ carriage inwards) − closing stock.

Direct labour: wages of production workers. Direct expenses: royalties, special tools, hire of special equipment for a job. Factory overheads: factory rent, power, insurance, depreciation of factory machinery and equipment, supervisor's salary, repairs, lighting, heating, cleaning, security, lubricants, small tools and consumable stores.
Work in progress (WIP): goods that are begun but not finished. Opening WIP is added; closing WIP is deducted.

Raw materials 1 January ₦40,000 and 31 December ₦48,000; purchases ₦250,000; carriage inwards ₦12,000; factory wages ₦180,000; direct labour ₦45,000; royalties ₦15,000; factory rent ₦60,000; factory power ₦35,000; factory insurance ₦18,000; depreciation of factory machinery ₦25,000; factory supervisor's salary ₦80,000; factory repairs ₦22,000; work in progress 1 January ₦30,000 and 31 December ₦35,000.

head: Manufacturing account
rows: Less closing stock of raw materials

p: The cost of production of ₦729,000 takes the place of purchases in the trading account. Sales ₦1,200,000. Opening stock of finished goods ₦50,000 + cost of production ₦729,000 = ₦779,000. Less closing stock of finished goods ₦60,000 = cost of goods sold ₦719,000. Gross profit = 1,200,000 − 719,000 = ₦481,000.
The manufacturing account produces a COST. The trading account uses that cost and compares it with sales to find the gross profit.

Raw materials stock and work in progress appear in the manufacturing account. Finished goods stock appears in the trading account. In the balance sheet, all three are current assets and are listed under stock.

Putting office rent or sales commission in the manufacturing account (they belong in the profit and loss account). Putting finished goods stock in the manufacturing account. Forgetting work in progress. Using purchases alone instead of raw materials consumed. Not transferring the cost of production to the trading account.
